lesson_title: The Taxi Queue: Longitudinal Waves and Sound
hook_text: Someone bumps the back of the taxi queue — and the bump reaches the front without anyone walking there.
clip_script: Friday afternoon, long queue at the rank. Someone at the back bumps the person in front. That person stumbles into the next, who bumps the next, and a squash runs all the way to the front. Nobody walked. Everyone shuffled and settled back into their spot. That squash is a compression — people packed tighter than usual. And right behind it, where everyone got pushed forward, the queue is stretched thin: that's a rarefaction. Now here is the whole definition. The people moved forward and back ALONG the same line the squash travelled. Not across it — along it. That is what longitudinal means. Swap the people for air molecules and you have sound, exactly. Something vibrates, squashes the air, pulls back, leaves a thin patch — and squashes run out through the room until one hits your eardrum and pushes it in. Which is why space is silent. No particles, nothing to squash, no sound. And the tighter the queue, the faster the squash: steel about five thousand metres a second, water fifteen hundred, air three hundred and forty. That last number is why you count between the lightning and the thunder.
visual_style: A busy South African taxi rank at golden hour, the queue drawn as a line of figures with a bright band of compression travelling up it; the figures dissolve into air molecules, then into a bell jar going silent.
mood: Everyday street energy sharpening into a clean physical insight.
pacing: Quick jostling rhythm through the queue, a held silent beat on the vacuum, brisk numbers to close.
